prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LAHORE, Pakistan (CNN) -- His job was to drive the bus. But Meher Mohammad Khalil is now being hailed as a lifesaver. On Wednesday Meher Mohammad Khalil went back to the place where gunmen attacked his bus. When gunmen jumped out of bushes and began spraying bullets at the bus carrying the Sri Lankan cricket team Tuesday, Khalil quickly sized up his options and got everyone to safety. "First I thought there were some firecrackers going off. Then, when I saw the elite force cars in front of me taking fire, I immediately lost my voice," Khalil told CNN on Wednesday. "At that time, the other elite car that was with us gave me cover, and then, when I saw he was giving me cover, my courage and my patience returned.  Watch CNN's interview with Khalil » . "I decided to take the vehicle from there, and one way or another, even if I had to drive over someone, I would take this bus and escape."  Watch the gunmen attack » . Khalil returned to the scene of the attack in the Pakistani city of Lahore on Wednesday to honor those who were killed and to place flowers in their memory. One of the dead was Zafar Khan, a friend and fellow bus driver who had been in a vehicle behind Khalil. "My eyes filled with tears that these were people that I was eating with and who died in doing their duty." Khalil had been part of a convoy heading to Gaddafi Stadium, where the Sri Lankan cricket team was to continue a match against Pakistan. Six police officers were killed, in addition to Khalil's friend Khan who was driving a bus with the match umpires.  See where the attack happened » . The Sri Lankan cricketers praised Khalil's quick thinking and action, saying he saved their lives. Six team members were injured by broken glass and shrapnel. Team captain Mahela Jayawardene wrote on his Web site of Khalil: "He probably saved our lives, showing remarkable bravery in the face of direct gunfire to keep the bus moving." Crowds mobbed Khalil as he paid his respects at the place where his life changed in an instant. "He is a hero, a real hero, a real man of the people," a man in the crowd said. Private donors in Lahore have rewarded Khalil with 300,000 rupees (more than $3,000) -- a small fortune for a Pakistani bus driver. Today, Khalil says all he can feel is pain of the loss of life. And he called on the attackers to recognize that their victims are humans just like them, with mothers and sisters. "For God's sake, please stop this terrorism and let this nation breathe a sigh of relief," he said. CNN's Zein Basravi contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.output:
# The driver who kept moving: How Meher Mohammad Khalil saved Sri Lanka’s cricket team

**Lahore, Pakistan** — As gunfire erupted around the Sri Lankan cricket team’s bus on March 3, 2009, driver Meher Mohammad Khalil faced a split-second choice: stop or keep moving.

He pressed the accelerator.

Khalil steered the bus through an ambush by heavily armed militants near Lahore’s Gaddafi Stadium, carrying the players and team officials to safety as bullets struck the vehicle and explosions shook the road.

The Sri Lankan squad had been traveling to the stadium for the third day of a Test match against Pakistan when attackers armed with rifles, grenades and rocket launchers opened fire at Liberty Square. Several Sri Lankan players and staff members were wounded.

Six police officers and two civilians were killed in the assault. An officials’ vehicle traveling with the team was also attacked, leaving Pakistani umpire Ahsan Raza seriously injured.

Amid the chaos, Khalil remained at the wheel.

With the team taking cover inside the bus, he drove toward the stadium rather than stopping in the exposed intersection. The bus reached the venue, where the players were moved to safety before being evacuated from Pakistan by helicopter.

Khalil later said he had focused on only one task: getting his passengers out alive. His actions turned an ordinary bus driver into a national hero in Pakistan and a celebrated figure in Sri Lanka.

The Sri Lankan government invited him to the country and honored him for his bravery. Players and officials credited his composure with preventing an already deadly attack from becoming an even greater tragedy.

The assault had lasting consequences for Pakistan. International teams largely refused to tour the country for years, forcing Pakistan to play many of its home matches abroad. Test cricket did not return to Pakistan until 2019 — with Sri Lanka again playing a central role.

For Khalil, however, the defining moment remained those few minutes in Lahore: gunfire outside, frightened passengers behind him and an open road ahead.

He did not stop.

counterfactuals.output:
*The following is a first-person reconstruction based on the account of bus driver Meher Mohammad Khalil and the known facts of the March 3, 2009 attack.*

---

I had driven cricket teams through Lahore many times. That morning, the Sri Lankan players were behind me, talking quietly as we approached Liberty Roundabout on our way to Gaddafi Stadium.

Then the road erupted.

Men appeared with rifles, grenades and rocket launchers. Bullets struck the bus—glass shattered, players threw themselves to the floor, and voices cried out behind me. For an instant, instinct told me to stop. Then I understood: if the bus stopped, we would all die.

So I kept my foot down.

The policemen escorting us fought back. They placed themselves between the attackers and the bus, and several were killed doing it. I could hear shots hitting the vehicle, but I concentrated on the road ahead. I did not look back. I drove through the ambush and did not slow until we were inside Gaddafi Stadium.

Only then did I see the blood and broken windows. Several Sri Lankan players and officials had been wounded. Yet the team had escaped. People later called me a hero, but I never accepted that word easily. I had a steering wheel and an engine. The policemen outside had only their courage. Six police officers and two civilians lost their lives that day.

The attack ended international cricket in Pakistan for years. Stadiums that had once roared fell quiet, and teams stayed away. I carried the memory of that morning—the gunfire, the shattered glass, and the men who never came home.

When Sri Lanka eventually returned to play in Lahore, I returned too. It was more than a cricket match. To see a Sri Lankan team bus reach the stadium safely again was to see fear challenged and a wound begin to close.

I went back not to celebrate myself, but to remember those who had cleared our path with their lives. The applause belonged to them.

Cricket had returned. But before the first ball was bowled, I thought of the policemen at Liberty Roundabout—the men who made sure our bus kept moving.

**LAHORE, Pakistan —** As bullets and grenades struck the Sri Lankan cricket team’s bus near Lahore’s Gaddafi Stadium, driver Meher Mohammad Khalil made a split-second decision: he would not stop.

Gunmen attacked the convoy on March 3, 2009, killing six Pakistani police officers and two civilians. Several Sri Lankan players were wounded, including captain Mahela Jayawardene, Kumar Sangakkara, Thilan Samaraweera and Tharanga Paranavitana. Assistant coach Paul Farbrace was also injured.

Khalil later recalled that his only thought was to keep driving and get the team to safety. Players described lying on the floor as gunfire shattered windows and struck the bus.

“The bus driver was amazing,” Jayawardene said afterward, praising Khalil for continuing through the barrage and accelerating toward the stadium. “He just kept driving.”

Khalil’s quick action carried the team through the ambush and into the security of Gaddafi Stadium, a decision widely credited with preventing a far greater loss of life.

The driver was subsequently welcomed in Sri Lanka as a national hero. He received a combined cash reward reported at about **$21,000** from the Sri Lankan government, Sri Lanka Cricket and other donors, along with public honors recognizing his bravery.

Khalil consistently played down the acclaim, saying he had simply done his duty. For the cricketers aboard the bus, however, his composure under fire made him the man who brought them home alive.
